<reason>Side A built the more durable case: fusion's cost is a rounding error against energy budgets, spillovers and expertise decay are real, and private fusion is the harvest of public science. Side A's arithmetic rebuttal (A2.1) largely neutralized CON's load-bearing opportunity-cost argument, and the "budgets coexist" point survived B's counter about finite engineers and political capital, which was asserted but never grounded in magnitude. Side B's best live routes were the mid-century lock-in window and the "option with no expiry is faith" line; A answered the expiry question directly (failure = stagnation, not calendar) and blunted lock-in with the 2070-grid and prototype-in-2030s framing, though B's fission-in-15-years audit point was never fully met—A's closing quietly shifted the metric from grid electricity to bankability, a mild evasion. B was consistently punchy and disciplined, but A made the decisive clash easier to decide and controlled the weighing. Close, competitive debate; A wins on stronger comparative resolution.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over the "audit" standard: B's pressure question demanding a failure date led to A's "stagnation, not the calendar" answer, which B countered with the memorable "an option with no expiry is not finance, it is faith" — but A's earlier arithmetic showing fusion's few billions cannot be the marginal dollar blocking grid buildout did more structural damage to CON's core opportunity-cost case than any of B's responses repaired.</best_rebuttal>
